name: Technology Due Diligence
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Kicking the Tires: A Due Diligence Checklist for Believing a Technology Claim
lesson.summary: Technology due diligence is the structured process of verifying a technology's real maturity, evidence base, and track record before accepting its marketing story, and it turns base rate reasoning and Sagan's rule into an actual investigation you can run.
lesson.body:
Due diligence is a term borrowed from investing and law, where it means the reasonable investigation a person is expected to carry out before making a commitment, whether that is buying a company, signing a contract, or relying on a piece of evidence in court. Applied to technology, due diligence means the same thing: before you believe a claim, fund a project around it, or build a strategy on top of it, what would you actually go check?

The first and most important check draws directly on an idea covered earlier in this course: quantum computing's most dramatic headlines are often scientifically real but sit at a very early Technology Readiness Level, or TRL, a standard scale originally developed by NASA that runs from TRL 1, basic principles observed, up through TRL 9, proven in full operational deployment. A lot of the flashiest quantum computing news covers results at TRL 2 or 3, meaning a technology concept has been formulated or an experimental proof of concept has been demonstrated in a controlled lab setting, nowhere close to a deployable product. Due diligence starts by asking, plainly and regardless of the language used to describe it, what TRL is this claim actually at.

From there, a practical checklist follows. Read the primary source, the actual paper or technical report, rather than stopping at the press release or news summary written about it. Check who is making the claim and what they stand to gain from it: a startup mid funding round has different incentives than an academic lab publishing in a peer reviewed journal with no product to sell. Check whether the result has been independently replicated or verified by a third party, since a claim no one else has reproduced carries much less weight than one that has been checked. Check the actual numbers against the known roadmap of what still needs to be solved: a claim that solves one narrow piece of a much larger problem is more credible than one that claims to have solved everything at once, since solving everything at once is, by base rate, extremely rare. And check the claim's history: has this team, company, or field made similar claims before, and did those claims hold up on the stated timeline?

Consider a concrete example: a company announces it has achieved quantum advantage on a commercially useful problem. Due diligence asks a specific set of questions. Was the benchmark problem chosen because it happens to favor the quantum system's strengths, with little real world use on its own? Was the classical comparison run on genuinely optimized, current generation hardware, or against a weaker baseline chosen to make the gap look larger? Has any independent group reproduced the result? And what TRL does the underlying claim correspond to once the marketing language is stripped away? This same disciplined habit of checking, rather than accepting, is exactly what you will need later in this course when writing a defensible executive brief or running a full red team analysis, so treat it as the front line skill everything else in this closing stretch of the course builds on.
